feedback: If a learner 'wins' by sounding more certain, redirect to the evidence: strength comes from the test design, not the loudness of the claim.
If a learner cannot counter a weak anecdote, prompt: 'What stronger test could settle this — what would you compare against?'
Reinforce when a learner concedes because the other side's evidence is genuinely stronger.
activities.intendedInsight: Argument from evidence is a real exchange: you marshal evidence to support or refute, weigh an opponent's evidence by its design, and change your mind when the stronger evidence demands it.
learnerActions: Take a side in a spoken exchange where a partner (another learner, a teacher in role, or a scripted persona) advances a claim backed by weak evidence — e.g. a single anecdote.
Refute it with stronger evidence, naming why your evidence is stronger (controlled comparison, repeated trials).
Defend your own claim when the partner challenges it, and judge the quality of the evidence the partner offers rather than how confidently they speak.
Reach a reasoned position, revising it if the opponent's evidence turns out stronger.
activities.title: Debate the claim out loud

feedback: If relevance and strength get merged, split the two questions explicitly: first 'does this bear on the claim?', then 'how strong is it?'
If an assertion is counted as evidence, ask what was actually observed or measured to back it up.
When ranking, ask the learner to name the feature (controls, sample size, repetition) that moved an item up the ladder.
If a learner labels a reasoned judgement from research findings as mere opinion, distinguish it: reasoned judgement rests on gathered findings, whereas speculation or opinion does not.
With competing claims, prompt the learner to show that one card can support one claim while being irrelevant to or refuting the other.
activities.intendedInsight: Support-vs-refute, relevance, strength ranking, and telling facts from reasoned judgement and from speculation are separable judgements you can apply item by item — and the same evidence pool can bear differently on competing claims.
learnerActions: Categorise a set of evidence items for a given claim as supports / refutes / irrelevant.
Sequence several pieces of evidence from weakest to strongest and explain the ordering.
Given a mix of statements, sort them into three kinds — a fact/observation, a reasoned judgement based on research findings, and a speculation or bare opinion — and say how you can tell them apart.

Given two competing claims and a shared pool of evidence, decide for each piece which claim it supports, which it refutes, or whether it is irrelevant to both — then judge which claim the pool overall better supports.

As a quick warm-up, compare two short investigations and say whose evidence is stronger (controlled comparison with many trials vs a single uncontrolled observation); the full claim-vs-evidence reasoning is developed in the seed-sprouting check, so treat this as a brief classification, not a repeat of it.
activities.title: Sort, rank, and compare evidence across claims

feedback: If a learner says 'Aisha's is fine — her seed sprouted', ask what she compared against; with no no-food group, the sprouting could be coincidence.
If a learner treats the assertion itself as the evidence, split it explicitly into 'the claim' versus 'the observation that tests it' for each child.
If a learner judges by who sounds surer or by authority, point out that strength comes from the design (control, number of trials), not from the person or their confidence.

Full-credit response: separates claim from evidence, judges by controlled comparison and sample size, and explains when evidence supports or refutes — rating strength by structure, not agreement or confidence.
activities.intendedInsight: Evidence is judged by its structure — a controlled comparison with multiple trials — not by whether it agrees with the claim or by who sounds more confident. A single confirming observation is not proof.
learnerActions: Read two accounts: Aisha says 'It works — I used the plant food once and my seed sprouted.' Ben says 'I planted 20 seeds with the food and 20 without, same everything else, and the food ones sprouted two days sooner on average.'
Decide whose evidence is stronger and explain why in terms of test design.
For each child, state the difference between the CLAIM ('the food makes seeds sprout faster') and the EVIDENCE (what was observed and how it was gathered).

Answer probing follow-ups: What did Ben compare against that Aisha didn't, and why does that matter? Does Aisha's sprouted seed prove the food worked, or could something else explain it? If Ben's food-seeds and no-food-seeds had sprouted at the same time, would that support or refute the claim?
activities.title: Claim-versus-evidence check (seed sprouting)
